cards.title: Jesus Fashioning Live Birds from Clay in Infancy Gospel of Thomas 2
cards.note: Surah 3:49 presents Jesus declaring to the Sons of Israel that he will fashion the form of a bird from clay and breathe into it so that it becomes a living bird, matching the clay sparrows miracle in chapter 2 of the second-century Infancy Gospel of Thomas.

discussion.view: Traditional commentators state that the Quran preserves an authentic miracle from the childhood and ministry of Jesus that was left unrecorded in the four canonical Gospels.
discussion.reply: First-century New Testament writings contain no account of Jesus animating clay birds, and John 2:11 explicitly identifies turning water into wine at Cana as the first of His signs. The clay birds narrative first appears in the mid-second-century Greek Infancy Gospel of Thomas 2, alongside episodes of the child Jesus withering and striking down playmates.

cards.title: Mary Beneath the Date-Palm Fed by Dropping Dates and a Miraculous Stream
cards.note: Surah 19:22–25 depicts Mary resting exhausted beside the trunk of a date-palm, where a voice from beneath her commands a water stream to flow at her feet and bids her shake the palm trunk for fresh ripe dates, matching Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew 20.

discussion.view: Classical exegetes regard this scene as a divinely revealed account of Mary's solitary childbirth in the wilderness near Bethlehem.
discussion.reply: Canonical Luke 2:4–7 places Jesus's birth in Bethlehem with Joseph present, without a palm tree or water spring. The combined miracle of the date-palm bending its fruit to Mary and a spring opening from its roots appears in chapter 20 of the sixth-century Latin Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew during the Holy Family's later flight into Egypt.

cards.title: Iblis Refusing to Prostrate to Adam Because Fire Surpasses Clay
cards.note: Surah 7:11–18 narrates God commanding the angels to prostrate before Adam and Iblis refusing because he was created from fire whereas Adam was created from clay, matching the Latin Vita Adae et Evae 13–16 and the Syriac Cave of Treasures.

discussion.view: Muslim commentators present the command for the angels to bow to Adam and Iblis's boast of fiery origin over clay as the primeval account of Satan's fall at the dawn of creation.
discussion.reply: Genesis 1–3 contains no command for angels to bow to Adam and no dialogue with Satan about fire and clay. The narrative of God commanding the angels to worship the newly formed Adam comes from the apocryphal Life of Adam and Eve (Vita Adae et Evae 13–16), and Satan's specific boast that he is 'fire and spirit' refusing to bow to 'a thing of dust' appears in the Syriac Cave of Treasures.

cards.title: Mary Accused by Her People and Addressed as Sister of Aaron
cards.note: In Surah 19:27–28, Mary's people accuse her over her child and address her as 'Sister of Aaron' ('daughter of Imran' in 66:12), combining Protevangelium of James 15 with Miriam, sister of Aaron and daughter of Amram, in Exodus 15:20 and Numbers 26:59.

discussion.view: Muslim traditions (Sahih Muslim 2135) and classical commentators explain that Mary was called 'Sister of Aaron' either figuratively after a righteous Israelite man or because she belonged to the Levitical lineage of Aaron.
discussion.reply: In Hebrew and Arabic (`Maryam`), Mary Mother of Jesus and Miriam of the Exodus share the same name. The Quran calls Jesus's mother both 'Sister of Aaron' (19:28) and 'daughter of Imran' (66:12; 3:35), matching the biblical family triad of Miriam—daughter of Amram (`Imran`) and sister of Aaron in Numbers 26:59 and Exodus 15:20—who lived over a millennium before first-century Mary.

cards.title: Wife of Imran Dedicating Mary to the Temple and Angels Bringing Her Food
cards.note: Surah 3:35–37 narrates the wife of Imran vowing her unborn child to the sanctuary, naming her Mary, and Zachariah finding miraculous food with her in the prayer chamber, matching Anna's vow and Mary's temple upbringing in Protevangelium of James 4 and 8.

discussion.view: Muslim exegetes regard Mary's dedication to the Jerusalem sanctuary under the guardianship of the priest Zachariah and her miraculous out-of-season provisions as revealed prophetic biography.
discussion.reply: Under Mosaic law (Numbers 3:10; 18:1–7), residency and service inside the Temple sanctuary were restricted to male Levites and Aaronic priests, and canonical Gospels place Mary at home in Nazareth (Luke 1:26–28). The story of Mary's mother vowing her unborn child to the Temple and Mary living inside the sanctuary fed by an angel originates in the mid-second-century Greek Protevangelium of James 4:1 and 8:1.

cards.title: Crucifixion Substitution: They Did Not Kill Him, It Seemed So to Them
cards.note: Surah 4:157–158 states that Jesus was neither killed nor crucified, 'rather it was made to appear so to them (`shubbiha lahum`),' matching the docetic substitution accounts in Irenaeus (Against Heresies 1.24.4) and the Nag Hammadi treatises.

discussion.view: Classical Sunni commentators such as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that God cast the physical likeness of Jesus onto another person—such as a disciple or an enemy—who was crucified in his place while Jesus was raised bodily to heaven.
discussion.reply: First-century Christian, Jewish, and Roman sources (the Gospels, Paul, Tacitus in Annals 15.44, and Josephus in Antiquities 18.3.3) record Jesus's crucifixion under Pilate. The claim that a look-alike substitute was crucified while Jesus ascended unharmed originated in second-century Gnostic texts (Basilides in Irenaeus 1.24.4; Second Treatise of the Great Seth), which denied that a spirit could suffer in flesh.

cards.title: Demons in Solomon's Reign and the Two Angels Harut and Marut in Babylon
cards.note: Surah 2:102 links demons in Solomon's kingdom teaching magic with two angels in Babylon named Harut and Marut, combining 1 Enoch 7–8 on fallen angels teaching sorcery with Talmud Gittin 68a on Solomon's male and female demons.

discussion.view: Classical exegetes explain that Surah 2:102 exonerates Solomon of practicing sorcery while affirming that God sent two angels, Harut and Marut, to Babylon as a test regarding magic.
discussion.reply: The narrative combines three Near Eastern traditions: Talmudic legends in Gittin 68a giving Solomon authority over demons, the Second Temple Book of Watchers (1 Enoch 7–8) where angels descend and teach humans charms and root-cuttings, and the paired Zoroastrian archangels (`Amesha Spentas`) Haurvatat/Horvadad and Ameretat/Amerodad, whose Middle Persian names correspond philologically to Harut and Marut.

cards.title: Priests Casting Their Pens as Lots to Decide Who Will Guard Mary
cards.note: Surah 3:42–44 cites as unseen knowledge how the temple priests disputed and cast their pens or rods (aqlamahum) as lots to determine who would become Mary's guardian, matching the lot-casting in the Protevangelium of James 8:2–9:1.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the temple priests cast their reed pens into the Jordan River to settle their dispute over who would raise the child Mary after Zechariah claimed priority through his marriage to her maternal aunt.
discussion.reply: The canonical Gospels never place Mary's upbringing inside the Jerusalem Temple or mention a priestly lottery for her guardianship. That episode comes from the second-century Greek Protevangelium of James 8:2–9:1, where the high priest Zacharias summons the widowers to bring their rods to the Temple so a sign may designate who will take the virgin of the Lord into his keeping.

cards.title: Surah 5 Review of Jesus' Clay Birds, Healings, and Sorcery Accusation
cards.note: In God's direct address to Jesus in 5:110, breathing life into a clay bird stands alongside speaking in the cradle and the Israelites calling his signs 'clear magic,' matching the Infancy Gospel of Thomas 2:2–4 and Talmud Sanhedrin 43a.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read 5:110 as God's covenantal reminder to Jesus enumerating the miracles granted to him by divine permission (bi-idhni) to distinguish prophetic signs from divine sonship.
discussion.reply: Unlike 3:49, where Jesus announces these signs to Israel, 5:110 frames them as God's retrospective address and adds the Israelites' charge that his signs were 'clear magic.' That passage unites the second-century Infancy Gospel of Thomas 2:2–4 (animating clay sparrows) with the rabbinic verdict in Talmud Sanhedrin 43a that Jesus practiced sorcery and led Israel astray.

cards.title: Surah 38 Account of God's Two Hands Forming Clay Adam and Iblis's Boast
cards.note: In Surah 38:71–85, God asks Iblis why he refused to prostrate before 'what I created with My two hands,' and Iblis boasts that he was made from fire while Adam was made from clay, matching the Syriac Cave of Treasures and Vita Adae et Evae 14–15.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir state that God honored Adam by fashioning him from clay with His two hands and commanding the angels to perform a prostration of honor, which Iblis rejected through analogical pride comparing fire to clay.
discussion.reply: Distinctive to Surah 38 is God's rebuke concerning 'what I created with My two hands' alongside Iblis's fire-over-clay argument. Genesis 1–3 contains no angelic prostration to Adam, whereas the Syriac Cave of Treasures depicts God fashioning Adam with His holy hands and the fallen prince refusing to bow because he is fire and spirit while Adam is dust, alongside Vita Adae et Evae 14–15.

cards.title: Abraham Glancing at the Stars, Mocking Food Offerings, and the Furnace
cards.note: Surah 37:83–98 links three episodes: Abraham glancing at the stars and excusing himself as sick, mocking the food set before the silent idols before striking them, and being cast into a blazing furnace, combining Jubilees 12 and Bereishit Rabbah 38:13.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that Abraham looked at the stars to feign illness so his people would leave him alone in the idol temple during their festival, allowing him to mock their food offerings and smash the statues with his right hand.
discussion.reply: Distinctive to Surah 37 is the astrological glance at the stars (37:88) paired with mocking the food offered to the idols (37:91). These motifs combine the second-century BC Book of Jubilees 12:16–18 (where Abram observes the stars at night before rejecting astrology) with Bereishit Rabbah 38:13 (where a woman brings a dish of fine flour as an offering before Abraham smashes the idols and faces Nimrod's fire).

cards.title: Iblis Refusing to Bow to Adam Formed from Dry Clay and Dark Mud
cards.note: Surah 15:26–42 contrasts creating man from sounding dry clay of dark molded mud (salsalin min hama'in masnun) with creating the jinn from scorching fire before Iblis refuses to bow to Adam, matching the Cave of Treasures and Vita Adae et Evae 14–16.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir interpret salsalin min hama'in masnun in 15:26–33 as dried clay formed from dark, altered mud that makes a ringing sound when struck, contrasting Adam's earthen origin with the smokeless scorching flame of the jinn.
discussion.reply: Surah 15 is the sole Quranic passage to use the formula 'dry clay from dark molded mud' (salsalin min hama'in masnun) and 'fire of scorching wind' (nar al-samum). The narrative structure — God breathing His spirit into clay-formed Adam, the angels bowing, Iblis refusing to worship a creature of dust, and his banishment until the appointed time — parallels the Syriac Cave of Treasures and Vita Adae et Evae 14–16.

cards.title: Surah 2 Account of the Angels Bowing to Adam After the Naming Scene
cards.note: Immediately after Adam recites the names of all things before the angels in 2:31–33, Surah 2:34 narrates God commanding the angels to prostrate before Adam while Iblis refuses in arrogance, matching Vita Adae et Evae 13–15 and the Cave of Treasures.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that in 2:34 God commanded the angels to bow to Adam as a greeting of honor after Adam demonstrated superior knowledge by naming the creatures, whereas Iblis refused out of envy and pride.
discussion.reply: Unlike 7:12, 15:33, and 38:76, which give Iblis's fire-versus-clay argument, 2:34 places the command to prostrate immediately after Adam's naming of the creatures (2:31–33) and attributes Iblis's refusal simply to arrogance (istakbara). This sequence directly parallels the Syriac Cave of Treasures, where Adam names all creatures on his throne before the angels bow the knee and the rebellious archangel refuses.

cards.title: Surah 26 Dialogue of Abraham Asking Whether Terah's Idols Hear or Help
cards.note: In Surah 26:69–89, Abraham asks his father and people whether their idols hear them when they call or can benefit or harm them, and urges worship of the Creator who provides food and drink, reproducing Book of Jubilees 12:2–5.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir view Abraham's catechism in 26:70–74 as a prophetic demonstration showing the helplessness of carved statues and the insufficiency of blind ancestral imitation (wajadna aba'ana kadhalika yaf'alun).
discussion.reply: Unlike 21:51–70 and 37:83–98, Surah 26:69–89 omits the smashing of the idols and the fiery furnace, focusing on Abraham's verbal interrogation of his father over whether the idols hear prayers or bring profit (hal yasma'unakum idh tad'un aw yanfa'unakum). That exact question appears in the second-century BC Book of Jubilees 12:2–5 ('What help and profit have we from those idols... For there is no spirit in them').

cards.title: Mary and Her Son Sheltered on High Ground with a Flowing Spring
cards.note: Surah 23:50 states that God gave the son of Mary and his mother refuge on high ground with a restful hollow and a flowing spring (rabwatin dhati qararin wa-ma'in), combining the mountain refuge of Protevangelium 22 with the spring of Pseudo-Matthew 20.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report varying geographical identifications among early commentators for the 'high ground with a restful hollow and flowing spring' in 23:50, including Damascus, Ramla, Jerusalem, and Egypt during the flight from Herod.
discussion.reply: Unlike 19:23–26, where Mary gives birth alone beside a palm tree and a stream (sariyyan), 23:50 describes God sheltering both the son of Mary and his mother on high ground (rabwah) with a flowing spring. This combines the cleft mountain refuge of the Protevangelium of James 22 with the miraculous spring of water opened beneath the palm tree during the flight to Egypt in Pseudo-Matthew 20.

sources.en: And Elizabeth , having heard that they were searching for John, took him and went up into the hill-country, and kept looking where to conceal him. And there was no place of concealment. sources.en: Then Jesus said to it: Raise yourself, O palm tree, and be strong, and be the companion of my trees, which are in the paradise of my Father; and open from your roots a vein of water which has been hid in the earth, and let the waters flow, so that we may be satisfied from you. And it rose up immediately, and at its root there began to come forth a spring of water exceedingly clear and cool and sparkling. And when they saw the spring of water, they rejoiced with great joy , and were satisfied, themselves and all their cattle and their beasts. Wherefore they gave thanks to God .
